documentation: Top-level functions, scope functions, and kotlin.Result — everything declared directly in the `kotlin` package (not `kotlin.collections`/`kotlin.sequences`, which have their own manifests, and not `kotlin.math`/`kotlin.text`/`kotlin.ranges`, which have theirs). Audited directly against Emitter.kt's emitCall/emitMethodCallTarget dispatch, not assumed from memory.

declarations.name: TODO
limitations: No dedicated codegen — falls through to a literal call to an undefined Lua global TODO(), failing at runtime with 'attempt to call a nil value' instead of raising NotImplementedError

declarations.name: error
limitations: No dedicated codegen — happens to work by passing through to Lua's own real error(message) global, for the common single-string-argument case; doesn't construct/throw an IllegalStateException the way real Kotlin error() does

declarations.name: require
limitations: Falls through to a literal call to Lua's require(), which is the MODULE LOADER (this transpiler's own module system emits real require("...") calls for imports) — require(condition) passes a boolean where require() expects a module-name string, failing at runtime with "bad argument #1 to 'require'". A genuine name collision, not just a gap.

declarations.name: check
limitations: No dedicated codegen and no Lua global named check — compiles to a call to an undefined global, fails at runtime

declarations.name: requireNotNull
limitations: No dedicated codegen and no matching Lua global — compiles to a call to an undefined global, fails at runtime

declarations.name: checkNotNull
limitations: Same as requireNotNull() — no dedicated codegen, no matching Lua global

declarations.name: repeat
limitations: repeat is a Lua KEYWORD (repeat ... until), so falling through to the literal-passthrough fallback produces repeat(n, function() ... end) — a Lua SYNTAX ERROR, not just a wrong value. Worse than a plain gap.

declarations.name: assert
limitations: The simple 1-arg form happens to work via Lua's own real assert(v) global; the lazy-message trailing-lambda form assert(cond) { "msg" } breaks — the lambda value is passed as assert's message argument without ever being invoked/stringified

declarations.name: lazy
limitations: No dedicated codegen; `by` property-delegation syntax itself isn't lexed/parsed at all, so `val x by lazy { ... }` is a parse-time failure, not just unsupported codegen

declarations.name: runCatching
limitations: Only the single-lambda-argument call form is recognized; Result<T> isn't a real tracked generic type, just the fixed kotlin.Result pseudo-class

declarations.name: isSuccess
limitations: Works via plain field access against the runtime table ResultRuntime's __runCatching builds (which does have an isSuccess field) rather than any dedicated property binding

declarations.name: isFailure
limitations: Same plain-field-access caveat as isSuccess

declarations.name: getOrDefault
limitations: No dedicated codegen for this overload — only onSuccess/onFailure/getOrNull are routed to a runtime helper

declarations.name: run
declarations.documentation: Top-level, no-receiver form: `run { ... }` — a plain IIFE call, no runtime helper needed

declarations.name: run
declarations.documentation: Receiver form: `x.run { ... }` — binds the implicit receiver the same way `.apply` does

declarations.name: let
limitations: Only the single-lambda-argument call form is recognized; a user class defining its own method named `let` correctly takes priority over this built-in

declarations.name: also
limitations: Same single-argument-only caveat as let()

declarations.name: apply
limitations: Same single-argument-only caveat as let()

declarations.name: takeIf
limitations: Same single-argument-only caveat as let()

declarations.name: takeUnless
limitations: Same single-argument-only caveat as let()

declarations.name: with
limitations: Special-cased as a literal top-level 2-argument call (receiver, lambda) rather than a general dispatch; only recognized when written literally as with(x) { ... }

declarations.name: Int
declarations.documentation: Lua's single number type underneath; Int/Int division truncates toward zero via a generated __intdiv helper to match Kotlin semantics

declarations.name: Any
declarations.documentation: Also the fallback every unrecognized type name normalizes to

declarations.name: Long
limitations: Collapses to the same TypeName.INT as Int — no distinct 64-bit semantics, no overflow emulation; Lua 5.1 numbers are doubles underneath regardless

declarations.name: Short
limitations: Collapses to TypeName.INT, same as Long

declarations.name: Byte
limitations: Collapses to TypeName.INT, same as Long — no 8-bit wraparound

declarations.name: Float
limitations: Collapses to TypeName.DOUBLE — no distinct 32-bit precision

declarations.name: Char
limitations: No Char type exists anywhere in this subset — no single-quote character literal lexing, no distinct Char representation; character-like values go through single-character String values instead (e.g. kotlin.text.String.first()/last())

declarations.name: Nothing
limitations: Not a distinct type — collapses to Any like any other unrecognized name; no special never-returns typing

declarations.name: toString
limitations: Works correctly as a standalone call (tostring(...), with List/Set/Map bracket formatting) — the gap is that its STRING return type isn't tracked by the simplistic binary-expression type inferencer, so acc + x.toString() inside something like fold's accumulator (declared ANY, not STRING) can resolve the + to numeric arithmetic instead of string concatenation and fail at runtime with 'attempt to perform arithmetic on a string value'.

A second, separate gap found the same way: the List/Set/Map bracket formatting only fires when the value being printed is statically tracked as a List/Set/Map at the print call site. A List value fetched dynamically out of another collection (e.g. println(xs.groupBy { ... }[0]), or a chunked() sub-list) isn't tracked that way, so it prints as a raw table: 0x... address instead of [1, 2, 3] — the underlying data is still correct (confirmed via .size and real iteration), only the print representation degrades. Confirmed via a real interpreter run, not just reasoning about the code.

declarations.name: Array
limitations: No Array<T>/arrayOf(...) support at all — not even aliased onto List the way MutableList/ArrayList/HashSet/etc. are

declarations.name: T?
declarations.implementation: Parser.kt (trailing '?' on a type is parsed and discarded)
limitations: Purely cosmetic — there is no nullable-vs-non-null static type tracking anywhere; null-safety is handled only via the explicit runtime operators ?./?:/!!/as?, never via inferred nullability

declarations.name: genericTypeArguments
limitations: <T> type arguments on a type name or a call site are parsed and immediately discarded — no generics are tracked anywhere, so e.g. emptyList<Module>() and emptyList<Int>() compile identically

declarations.name: as
limitations: Parsed and fully discarded — 'Lua is dynamically typed and needs no cast' — so an incorrect cast never throws a ClassCastException the way real Kotlin does

declarations.name: as?
limitations: Same code path as as — the trailing ? is only tolerated syntactically. There is no runtime type check and no null-on-failure behavior; (x as? String) compiles to just x unchanged regardless of its real runtime type. A correctness gap, not merely a missing feature.
